purpose: The LITERATURE half of the decision-simulator factor ledger: what the research says about each factor and how the leading simulators implement it. /project-report Phase 7 reuses this and searches only the rows flagged needs_research or past the horizon.
status_is_not_stored: Deliberate. A factor's status in this model (IN / PARTIAL / INERT / ASC / OUT) is re-read at HEAD on every pass by grep of the registry and the Java. The model moves weekly; a status carried forward is a status that is wrong.
seeded_from: 20260907T013735_project_report.html (report-data block, read from 9cd8b4f before its deletion in 03b5220)

factors.what_research_says: Residential self-selection is a measured but minority share of the built-environment effect: disentangling it by housing type in one study put self-selection at 15.2%, 30.7%, 18.5% and 5.9% of the total impact on vehicle kilometres travelled for the four housing types examined, and the effect is modest for the elderly and large for younger adults. The built-environment side remains the Ewing-Cervero meta-analysis, with every 5D elasticity inelastic. A residence fixed from the census therefore carries most of the built-environment effect and mis-states only the self-selected minority.
factors.magnitude: literature: self-selection 6-31% of the total built-environment effect on VKT, varying by housing type; the remainder is the location itself
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: UrbanSim-class land-use models re-choose residence; ActivitySim, CT-RAMP, MATSim and eqasim all take residence from the synthetic population and never re-choose it during a run.
factors.query: Residential self-selection share of the built-environment effect in Australian cities (VISTA / Sydney HTS panel)

factors.what_research_says: Workplace location is a calibrated long-term choice in every activity-based practice: ActivitySim samples commute distances from regional distributions and selects zones to match them under land-use compatibility, then validates residence-to-work flows against the census commuting-flow table and the mandatory trip-length frequency distribution; where attractions are more reliable than the impedance the practice is doubly constrained (shadow-priced) so that both worker totals and job totals are held. The output check the field uses is the county-to-county (here LGA-to-LGA) flow table, not the mean distance.
factors.magnitude: unknown as a coefficient: the practice benchmark is an origin-destination flow table (census journey-to-work) and a trip-length distribution, not a central tendency
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim and CT-RAMP run a shadow-priced work location choice validated against census commuting flows; MATSim scenarios assign workplaces in the demand builder and hold them fixed.
factors.query: Australian activity-based model (AToM, Sydney STM) reported fit of modelled vs journey-to-work LGA flows - a transferable tolerance for own-LGA commute share

factors.what_research_says: Household car ownership is one of the strongest single predictors of mode: an increase in car ownership raises the probability of commuting by car and depresses active and transit modes, with a reported elasticity of -2.643 for the substitution of active modes. Income, household size, distance to centre, accessibility to shops/services/employment and intersection density are the dominant explanatory variables.
factors.magnitude: literature: elasticity of active-mode use with respect to car ownership approximately -2.6; income and household size the leading sociodemographic drivers
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP run an explicit auto-ownership choice model calibrated to observed auto sufficiency; MATSim scenarios usually take vehicles from the synthetic population and enforce availability through chain-based mode constraints rather than re-choosing ownership.
factors.query: A Vehicle ownership per household: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The e-bike evidence is now meta-analysed: across experimental studies, access to an e-bike adds about 5 km of daily travel and raises e-bike mode share by about 26 percentage points, while car use falls by about 2.4 km a day (a 10% drop in car mode share); single controlled trials report car share falling 21%, and older meta-studies put e-bike-for-car substitution at 43% of trips and 63% of mileage. The effect is context-dependent: where cycling is already high the e-bike substitutes conventional cycling; where it is low it draws from car and public transport. (Figures are abstract-level; the full text was not retrievable this pass.)
factors.magnitude: literature: +5 km/day travelled and +26 pp e-bike share with e-bike access; car -2.4 km/day (~-10% car share); substitution 43% of car trips in earlier syntheses
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim's bicycle contrib carries an e-bike as a vehicle type with its own speed and gradient response; no production city model draws an e-bike or EV ownership decision - both enter as a share of the fleet.
factors.query: E-bike share of Australian bicycle fleet and its effect on feasible cycling distance (NCPS 2023 e-bike ownership)

factors.what_research_says: Licence holding among people under 35 has fallen across Australia, the UK, the US, Canada and much of Europe: TfNSW reports 65.4% of 16-20 year olds licensed in 2017, 8.3 points below 2001 and 8.1 below 2009, with the proportion licensed at age 30 also declining cohort on cohort. The travel-behaviour consequence named is a greater reliance on getting a lift, especially in wealthy suburbs and high-car-ownership families, and more public transport, walking and cycling in less wealthy areas.
factors.magnitude: literature: 16-20 licence rate 65.4% (2017 NSW), down ~8 points on 2001; effect is a shift toward being a car passenger and toward PT/active modes
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP treat licence holding inside the auto-ownership and person-type models; MATSim scenarios encode it as a person attribute gating car as a chain-based mode.
factors.query: A Licence holding: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: A smartcard natural experiment on Dutch fares separates pass holders from single-ticket users: passengers on a monthly or annual subscription have the highest travel frequency per origin-destination pair per week - almost twice that of single-ticket users - and the estimated fare elasticities split cleanly between the frequent-user products (pay-as-you-go, student and subscription) and the occasional ones (end-of-month and single tickets). A pass converts the fare from a per-trip price to a zero marginal cost, and the behavioural response is the frequency, not the mode.
factors.magnitude: literature: subscription holders travel about 2x as often per OD pair as single-ticket users; fare elasticity differs by product class
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry a per-person fare class or pass flag into the cost term; MATSim fare handlers (as here) price per trip and per day-cap, so a pass has to be expressed as a zero marginal fare for the holder.
factors.query: Opal Gold Senior / concession share of Hunter bus and rail boardings (TfNSW patronage by card type)

factors.what_research_says: Ownership is high and use is low, and the two are only weakly coupled: the National Cycling Participation Survey (2011-2019) finds more than half of Australian households own at least one bicycle while cycling is 1.4% of daily travel; Melbourne apartment households own 0.86 bicycles on average, off-street bicycle parking more than doubles the odds a household owns one, and the correlation between household bicycles and regional cycling use is 0.238. Ownership is male, younger, more educated and higher-income; renting, apartment living and foreign origin reduce it.
factors.magnitude: literature: >50% of households own a bicycle against 1.4% cycling mode share (NCPS); 0.86 bikes per apartment household; ownership-use correlation 0.24
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim implementations gate bike by a household bicycle flag where the survey carries it; MATSim scenarios (as here) draw an availability rate per person and let mode choice decide use; no production model estimates an ownership choice.
factors.query: NCPS 2023 household bicycle ownership rate for NSW regional cities and the share of owners who rode in the last week

factors.what_research_says: Daily travel budgets are strikingly stable: the Sydney Household Travel Survey reports an average 81 minutes travelling per person per day and 24-30 km per person per day across regions, with average travel time steady over the reporting series while mode composition moved (weekday train trips +3.1%, bus +2.4%, walk-only +2.7%, vehicle driver -0.8%, passenger -0.2%).
factors.magnitude: literature: ~81 min/person/day travelling, 24-30 km/person/day (NSW HTS); the time budget is stable while mode composition moves
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP generate a full daily activity pattern per person from estimated models; MATSim takes chains as an input and mutates only times and modes during the run.
factors.query: B Activity generation and scheduling: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Joint and partially joint travel is a material share of household tours: partially joint tours - where one or more passengers is dropped off or picked up mid-tour - make up close to 14% of all tour types in metropolitan areas, and households with more than one student at the same school very commonly serve them on one car tour.
factors.magnitude: literature: partially joint tours ~14% of all tour types
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: CT-RAMP models joint tours explicitly (participation, party composition, destination); ActivitySim carries the same joint-tour chain; MATSim has no native joint-tour construct and scenarios add it as a contrib or in the demand builder.
factors.query: B Joint household decisions: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Escorting is modelled in practice as a nested choice: school tours split into outbound and inbound half-tours, each with pure escort / ridesharing / no escort and up to three household chauffeurs. Significant determinants are the chauffeur's employment status, age and flexibility at work, the child's age, household characteristics and the relative distances between home, school and workplace; mothers working longer hours and further from home are less likely to chauffeur.
factors.magnitude: literature: three escort alternatives per half-tour, up to three candidate chauffeurs; chauffeur work hours and job distance are the leading determinants
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: CT-RAMP and ActivitySim implement a dedicated school-escort model with chauffeur assignment; MATSim carries no escort construct natively.
factors.query: B Escort of children: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Telework reduces commuting and business trips, most clearly for full-time teleworkers, but the effect on TOTAL distance is mixed and design-dependent: rebound effects (extra non-work trips) and residential relocation to longer commutes offset part of the saving, and one-worker households increase total travel - particularly by car - while two-worker households show no significant increase.
factors.magnitude: literature: commute trips reduced; total distance effect ambiguous with documented rebound and relocation offsets
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim implementations added post-pandemic work-from-home models as a person-level choice feeding the daily activity pattern; MATSim scenarios usually encode it by removing work activities from a share of plans.
factors.query: B Telework / work-from-home: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Weekend travel has a different shape, not just a different volume: the sharp early-morning and mid-afternoon weekday peaks are absent on the weekend day because so few trips are to and from work, and social-recreational and personal-business travel spread more evenly across the day become the dominant influence; weekend travel raises car-pooling for both youth and adults but has no measured effect on transit use, and destination land use shifts toward residential.
factors.magnitude: literature: weekend day loses both commute peaks; purpose mix shifts to social/recreational; carpooling up, transit unchanged (NHTS 2009)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: CT-RAMP and ActivitySim are weekday models by default with separate weekend estimation where funded; MATSim scenarios build a weekend day from a separate plans file and timetable, as this model does for SAT and SUN.
factors.query: NSW HTS weekend vs weekday trip rate and purpose mix for the Hunter (published table)

factors.what_research_says: People with a travel-limiting disability are 8-10% of the population and make fewer trips - about 18.6% fewer overall in the Utah household survey, with the disparity largest on transit (4.21 against 5.71 trips a day) and smallest for driving alone - and they choose differently: a measured shift toward car-pooling, a lower value of travel time, and a transit share that stays low despite a 50% fare concession because access, not price, is the barrier.
factors.magnitude: literature: ~8-10% of the population; ~19% fewer trips; transit trips 4.21 vs 5.71 per day; shift to car passenger
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim implementations carry a disability flag into person type where the survey supports it; MATSim scenarios seldom represent it, and this model synthesises the flag without a consumer.
factors.query: ABS SDAC 2022 share of Hunter residents with a mobility limitation and their trip rate relative to others

factors.what_research_says: The practice is settled on size terms: each destination alternative's utility is a set of impedance terms plus one size function, where the size term is total or industry-specific employment for work, school enrolment for education, and for non-work purposes only the relevant categories - retail employment for shopping, restaurant employment for meals - with households or population for social purposes. Estimation results then show purpose-specific impedance coefficients (e.g. -0.01 business to -0.11 daily shopping per minute in one reported model) around a shared size term.
factors.magnitude: literature: size term = log of a weighted sum of purpose-relevant employment/enrolment/households; impedance coefficients purpose-specific, roughly -0.01 to -0.11 per minute in a reported estimation
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP estimate the size-term weights per purpose from the survey; MATSim demand builders (as here) declare them and validate against a job distribution.
factors.query: Estimated size-term weights by employment category for an Australian ABM (AToM / Sydney STM)

factors.what_research_says: The gravity/spatial-interaction relationship declines with distance, time and cost; the two competing deterrence forms are the power law and the negative exponential, with the negative exponential generally the preferred form in transport application, and the estimated deterrence parameter is sensitive to the spatial arrangement of the study area.
factors.magnitude: literature: negative-exponential deterrence generally preferred over power law; parameter is context- and geometry-sensitive rather than transferable
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Four-step and gravity models fit a per-purpose deterrence function; ActivitySim replaces it with a logsum-based destination utility; MATSim inherits whatever the demand builder produced.
factors.query: C Distance decay: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: A doubly constrained model preserves both the origin and destination totals from trip generation while a singly constrained one preserves origins only; doubly constrained is the appropriate form where the attraction totals are more reliable than the friction factors, and the standard case for work location, where predicted flows should equal both worker totals and job totals - in activity-based practice this is implemented as shadow pricing on the work and school location choices.
factors.magnitude: literature: no coefficient - a structural choice; doubly constrained (shadow-priced) is standard for work and school, singly constrained for discretionary purposes
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP shadow-price work and school location to hit zone job and enrolment totals; MATSim demand builders (as here) balance arrivals iteratively.
factors.query: Reported shadow-price convergence tolerance for ActivitySim work location (share of zones within x% of jobs)

factors.what_research_says: Short trips are systematically undercounted in travel surveys - the undercount concentrates on short walking, cycling and car trips for shopping and leisure, and every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walks to stops and car parks. More than 80% of walk trips are under 2 km, and walking and cycling behave as substitutes below 2 km.
factors.magnitude: literature: >80% of walk trips are under 2 km; walk trips systematically undercounted in survey targets; walk and bike substitute below 2 km
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP handle intrazonal trips with an intrazonal impedance term and micro-zone allocation; MATSim simulates them physically on the real network if the network resolution allows it.
factors.query: C Intra-zonal trips: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Departure time is a genuine choice, not a fixed profile: Small (1982) tied departure-time choice to a workplace constraint in the utility function, and travellers were willing to shift one to two minutes toward the early side, or one-third to one minute toward the late side, to save one minute of travel time.
factors.magnitude: literature: willingness to shift 1-2 min early, or 1/3-1 min late, per minute of travel time saved (Small 1982)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP model tour departure-time choice by purpose; MATSim mutates departure times each iteration under TimeAllocationMutator and prices the result through the scoring function.
factors.query: D Departure-time profile by purpose: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The schedule-delay cost function is asymmetric: the unit cost of arriving late exceeds the unit cost of arriving early, the disutility falls linearly to zero as arrival approaches the desired time, and Small hypothesises a FIXED penalty component on the late side - arriving late is always bad, however slightly.
factors.magnitude: literature: late-arrival unit cost strictly greater than early; a fixed late penalty on top of the linear term
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim prices exactly this pair as scoring.lateArrival and scoring.earlyDeparture against an activity's typical and opening/closing times; ActivitySim carries it inside time-of-day choice utilities.
factors.query: D Schedule delay / activity duration preferences: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: In-vehicle time and value of time by purpose
factors.what_research_says: The value of travel time savings is the single best-evidenced coefficient in the field, established by repeated international meta-analysis, and it scales with income: a meta-analysis of 268 income elasticities from 49 studies (1968-2019) puts the income elasticity of VTTS at 0.67 (OLS), 0.77 (WLS) and 0.80 (random effects), below the unity convention still used in appraisal.
factors.magnitude: literature: income elasticity of VTTS approximately 0.7-0.8, below the appraisal convention of 1.0; VTTS itself is purpose-specific by construction
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry purpose-specific VOT directly in the mode-choice utility; MATSim cannot - it scores per MODE, so a purpose-specific VOT has to be collapsed or pushed into per-person money sensitivity.
factors.query: E In-vehicle time and value of time by purpose: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Access, egress, wait and transfer time weights
factors.what_research_says: Out-of-vehicle time is valued well above in-vehicle time, and the multipliers are the best-established transferable numbers in the field. Wardman et al. report walk-time multipliers of 1.45 for urban and 1.70 for inter-urban trips and wait-time multipliers of 1.50 and 1.76 respectively; the 2026 update assembles 2,872 multipliers from 606 studies across 52 countries, 1963-2023, covering walk, wait, headway, displacement, reliability and congested time.
factors.magnitude: literature: walk-time multiplier ~1.45 urban (1.70 inter-urban), wait-time multiplier ~1.50 urban (1.76 inter-urban), relative to in-vehicle time
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP put these multipliers straight into the mode-choice utility; MATSim expresses them as the difference between a mode's marginalUtilityOfTraveling and the performing rate, plus utilityOfLineSwitch for transfers.
factors.query: E Access, egress, wait and transfer time weights: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Public transport demand is fare-inelastic in the short run and considerably more elastic in the long run: the recurring central tendencies are about -0.3 short run and -0.6 to -1.1 long run, with a meta-analysis reporting -0.24 short run against -1.1 long run and Schimek reporting -0.3/-0.7 across a large cross-section of US agencies.
factors.magnitude: literature: short-run PT fare elasticity approximately -0.3 (range -0.24 to -0.4); long-run -0.6 to -1.1
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP carry fares as a cost term divided by an income-segmented VOT; MATSim prices fares through a money-event handler and one marginalUtilityOfMoney, optionally per person.
factors.query: E Fares and money (income-scaled): literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Underpriced parking generates cruising, and cruising is a large share of central-area traffic: studies between 1927 and 2001 found 3.5-14 minutes to find a curb space and 8-74% of traffic cruising, with more recent work above 70%, and search time reaching up to 40% of total travel time. Shoup's operational rule is that a price producing roughly one vacancy in eight (a 12.5% vacancy rate) drives search time to zero.
factors.magnitude: literature: 3.5-14 min search time in congested centres; 8-74% of central traffic cruising; 12.5% vacancy as the price target that removes search
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: PTV Visum/Aimsun and MATSim's parking contribs simulate search explicitly against facility occupancy; ActivitySim prices parking as a cost term with a separate terminal-time component.
factors.query: E Parking cost and search time: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Road pricing is demand-elastic at the cordon: estimates for several cities put congestion reductions in the 10 to >30% range if a small share of peak traffic shifts; Singapore's ERP removed ~25,000 peak-hour vehicles and raised average speeds ~20%; a dynamic-pricing corridor simulation moved traffic density by 10-12% across the elasticity range; and the most recent live cordon recorded a 6.3% fall in vehicles entering (about 44,000 a day) against larger projections - real responses are often below the forecast.
factors.magnitude: literature: cordon or corridor pricing cuts affected traffic ~6-30% depending on charge and alternatives; first-year observed responses sit at the low end of forecasts
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim's roadpricing contrib and Aimsun/Visum toll models price links directly; ActivitySim carries tolls in the cost term with a VOT.
factors.query: Meta-analysis of toll elasticities of traffic volume (Australian toll roads, e.g. Sydney M-series)

factors.factor: Car availability and competition for household cars
factors.what_research_says: Car availability is the binding constraint on mode, not a preference: the elasticity of active-mode use with respect to car ownership is about -2.6, and the resource logic is that a chain-based mode can only be used if the vehicle is where the traveller left it. Household competition for a limited fleet is what converts a licensed non-driver into a passenger.
factors.magnitude: literature: elasticity of active-mode substitution with respect to car ownership approximately -2.6; car availability dominates person attributes in every reviewed model
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim enforces it structurally through chain-based modes in SubtourModeChoice - a mode is offered only if the resource is not conjured out of thin air; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP enforce it through auto-sufficiency segmentation in mode choice.
factors.query: E Car availability and competition for household cars: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Age and sex segment travel in direction more than in coefficient: older Australians drive, walk and use taxis and make little use of bicycles, rideshare or public transport; car use declines with age and dependence on transit rises as ability to drive falls; older women are the group most likely to use public transport; the 'gender turnaround' finds young women now travelling more than young men. No transferable coefficient was recovered.
factors.magnitude: unknown (direction established: car falls and PT/taxi/walk rise with age; women more PT; no central tendency)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP segment utilities by person type and age band; MATSim carries subpopulation-specific scoring.
factors.query: Estimated age and sex coefficients in an Australian mode choice model (Sydney STM or AToM)

factors.what_research_says: Income raises the value of time sub-proportionally: the meta-analysis of 268 elasticities puts the income elasticity of VTTS at 0.67-0.80, below the unity convention, and income is directly connected to vehicle ownership with higher-income households more inclined to drive alone and less interested in non-motorised modes.
factors.magnitude: literature: income elasticity of VTTS approximately 0.7-0.8 (0.67 OLS, 0.77 WLS, 0.80 RE)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP segment VOT by income band; MATSim's income-dependent scoring sets a per-person marginalUtilityOfMoney as (average income / personal income)^exponent.
factors.query: E Person attributes: income: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Built form: density, diversity, design, distance to transit
factors.what_research_says: Ewing and Cervero's meta-analysis of the built-environment literature to 2009 is the benchmark: VMT per capita is most strongly related to destination accessibility and secondarily to street-network design; walking relates most strongly to land-use diversity, intersection density and destination counts within walking distance; bus and train use relate equally to proximity to transit and network design, with diversity secondary. Critically, travel is generally INELASTIC with respect to every built-environment measure.
factors.magnitude: literature: all 5D elasticities are inelastic (|e| < 1); destination accessibility dominates VMT, diversity and intersection density dominate walking
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP put density, diversity and intersection density into destination and mode utilities as explicit terms; MATSim represents them physically through the network and land use rather than as coefficients.
factors.query: E Built form: density, diversity, design, distance to transit: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Most commute tours are simple: about 80% of US work tours fall into seven dominant patterns and the remaining 20% spread over 106 more complex ones, half of transit work tours are complex, and NHTS defines chaining as at least one intermediate stop between anchors (stays over 30 min); telecommuters make more stops per tour. Discretionary tours are more sensitive to environment than mandatory ones.
factors.magnitude: literature: ~20% of work tours complex (NHTS 2009); half of transit work tours complex
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: CT-RAMP/ActivitySim model stop frequency and location explicitly; MATSim inherits the chain and moves whole subtours.
factors.query: NSW HTS share of tours with an intermediate stop by purpose (published or derivable table)

factors.what_research_says: Crowding is priced as a time multiplier and the evidence base is large: Wardman and Whelan's synthesis of 208 valuations from 17 British studies over 20 years gives an average seated multiplier of 1.19 and an average standing multiplier of 2.32, with 124 standing observations ranging 0.94-6.05 and 84 seated ranging 1.00-1.78. The standing multiplier is of the same order as the walk and wait multipliers.
factors.magnitude: literature: seated crowding multiplier ~1.19, standing ~2.32 (208 valuations, 17 studies)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: PTV Visum and Emme price crowding inside transit assignment; MATSim requires an explicit capacity-dependent scoring extension (a contrib) - it is not in core scoring.
factors.query: E Crowding (seated / standing): literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Both are valued and both are established. The reliability ratio - the value of travel time variability divided by the value of travel time savings, measured against the standard deviation - lies between 0.8 and 1.3 with a value around 1.0 plausible. Headway elasticity of ridership is estimated at -0.263 to -0.277 in disaggregate analysis.
factors.magnitude: literature: reliability ratio 0.8-1.3 (~1.0 central); headway elasticity of ridership approximately -0.26 to -0.28
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP include a reliability term where data supports it; MATSim reproduces headway physically from the timetable but has no native reliability disutility.
factors.query: E Reliability and headway: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Weather matters mainly for cycling: its impact on mode choice is marginal overall, with cycling the most affected mode in every spatial setting and walking consistently less sensitive than cycling; a 10% change in cycling volume corresponds to about a 4.0-4.4 K temperature change, ~1 mm of precipitation, or 7.1 m/s of wind gust. Habit is stronger than the rational factors: psychological (rational and habitual) factors influence mode choice more than socio-economic ones, and habit explains behaviour better than rational evaluation.
factors.magnitude: literature: ~4.0-4.4 K temperature change or ~1 mm precipitation per 10% change in cycling volume; habit outweighs rational factors in the reviewed choice models
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: No production city simulator prices habit or weather in the base case; weather appears in research variants of MATSim and SUMO and in bike-demand models, not in appraisal models.
factors.query: E Comfort, safety, habit, weather, scenery: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Cyclists trade distance for stress at large, well-measured rates: on average cyclists travel 67% longer to include a cycle path facility, weekend cyclists up to 40% longer, and cyclists accept a 25-38% detour to avoid segments with high near-crash rates. Level of Traffic Stress integrates infrastructure type, road hierarchy, traffic volume and speed limit into one indicator, alongside BCI, BSL and HCM6. Cyclists are highly sensitive to traffic volume where no separate infrastructure exists.
factors.magnitude: literature: detour tolerance 25-38% to avoid high-stress segments; up to 67% longer to include a cycle path
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim's bicycle contrib scores infrastructure and gradient on the link; SUMO and Aimsun represent cycling physically without a stress disutility; ActivitySim carries bike-specific impedance in the mode utility.
factors.query: E Bike: stress (traffic), gradient, e-bike: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Walk: footway width, gradient, crossings, directness
factors.what_research_says: Pedestrians are sensitive to network attributes, crossing aids and street/block-face environment, and are willing to divert for better facilities but with limited detour tolerance. Slope directly influences walking effort and route choice, but terrain is perceived as a barrier only when very steep and then only uphill. Distance decay is steep: Walk Score applies no decay within 400 m (5 min) and a 12% decay from 400 to 1,600 m; mean walking access distances to rail stations of 756-805 m are reported for Europe and North America, with Australians willing to walk a little further.
factors.magnitude: literature: no decay under 400 m, ~12% decay 400-1,600 m; mean rail access walk 756-805 m; gradient binds only on steep uphill
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim can route walk on a real footway network with gradient-adjusted speeds (as here) or teleport it; ActivitySim uses a walk-accessibility skim; SUMO simulates pedestrians physically.
factors.query: E Walk: footway width, gradient, crossings, directness: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Ride: pairing, lifts, detour, wait for driver
factors.what_research_says: The lift is a household object: in the Greater Montreal origin-destination surveys (1987-2003), where passengers named their driver, approximately 70% of all car-passenger trips were intra-household ridesharing, and around 15% of those trips were generated exclusively for the passenger's purpose - a serve trip that creates its own return - with that share rising over the series. Ride-hailing pooling is a separate decision with its own determinants.
factors.magnitude: literature: ~70% of car-passenger trips are household lifts; ~15% of those are pure serve trips generating a return
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: No mainstream platform pairs the household lift physically: CT-RAMP/ActivitySim carry car-passenger as a share with an occupancy factor, MATSim scenarios teleport it. Physical pairing is what this project does that the field does not.
factors.query: Detour and wait tolerance for a household lift (minutes) from a chauffeuring or escort study

factors.factor: Taxi / rideshare: wait, fleet, refusal, surge
factors.what_research_says: Ride-hailing demand is price-sensitive but the estimates are wide: reported price elasticities range from -0.186 (UberX, Houston) through mean point estimates of -0.57 across four US markets to -2.22 in elastic settings, with demand most elastic on daytime weekends and least elastic in off-peak weekday hours. Riders trade price against wait time and are LESS price-sensitive and more wait-sensitive in rush hours and office-dense destinations; fare setting and wait time are simultaneous through network externalities, so a simple elasticity understates the response.
factors.magnitude: literature: ride-hailing price elasticity central estimate about -0.57 (range -0.19 to -2.22); wait-time sensitivity rises in peaks
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim's DRT/taxi contribs and BEAM simulate the fleet, dispatch and wait physically; ActivitySim represents TNC as a mode with a zonal wait-time skim.
factors.query: E Taxi / rideshare: wait, fleet, refusal, surge: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The motorcycle literature review finds psychological factors - rational and above all habitual - influence mode choice more strongly than socio-economic factors, with habit the better explanation of the two. The recurring determinants are travel time, destination distance, car availability, commuting distance and household income; males prefer cars and motorcycles, higher-income travellers prefer cars, lower-income travellers bicycle and bus. Public-transport quality in the catchment shifts motorcyclists measurably.
factors.magnitude: literature: habit dominates rational factors; car availability, distance and income are the leading observable determinants
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Almost no Western city model simulates motorcycles as a separate physical mode; the Asian ABM literature (and SUMO/Aimsun in motorcycle-dependent cities) treats them as a distinct vehicle class with its own PCE.
factors.query: E Motorbike: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Bus demand responds to both price and service, and both responses are inelastic in the short run: fare elasticity about -0.3 short run and -0.6 to -1.1 long run, headway elasticity of ridership -0.263 to -0.277. Access is the other half - walk access to stops carries the 1.45 walk multiplier, so stop spacing enters the utility at 1.45 times its clock time.
factors.magnitude: literature: bus fare elasticity ~-0.3 short run; headway elasticity ~-0.26 to -0.28; walk access valued at ~1.45x in-vehicle time
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every platform in the field simulates bus from a GTFS timetable; the differentiators are whether dwell responds to boardings and whether crowding is priced.
factors.query: E Bus: frequency, stop access, fares: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Transit signal priority produces large, repeatedly measured delay reductions for the priority vehicle and small costs to cross traffic: 53% and 43% reductions in average bus delay at two studied intersections against 14% and 16% increases in major-phase delay, and in Toronto TSP reduced transit delay 30-40% and travel time 2-6%. Dwell follows the TCQSM linear form - a base plus per-boarding and per-alighting service times; one calibrated model gives a 5.14 s base, 3.48 s per boarding and 1.70 s per alighting, with TCQSM service times of 4.5 s (exact change), 2 s (visual inspection) and 1.75 s (no fare payment).
factors.magnitude: literature: TSP cuts priority-vehicle delay 30-53% and travel time 2-6%; dwell approximately 5.1 s base + 3.5 s per boarding + 1.7 s per alighting
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Aimsun, Vissim and SUMO implement TSP as a controller behaviour; MATSim requires the signals contrib, which this project runs.
factors.query: E Light rail: tram priority, dwell: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Heavy rail: capacity, fare, station access
factors.what_research_says: Station access is the binding factor and it is not simply nearest-station: for trips needing an intermodal transfer, riders select the nearest rail station in only 40% of cases; mean walking access distances of 756-805 m are reported, with park-and-ride the dominant access mode at most suburban stations, and faster access modes enlarge the catchment - cycling access can raise train market share by over 10 percentage points at certain access distances.
factors.magnitude: literature: nearest station chosen in only ~40% of intermodal trips; mean walk access 756-805 m; cycle access can add >10 percentage points of train share
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Emme/Visum use station-choice and access-mode sub-models; MATSim routes access physically through the transit router's search and extension radii.
factors.query: E Heavy rail: capacity, fare, station access: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Ferry ridership is the mode the literature says cannot be forecast from time and cost alone: water-transit riders choose their mode on factors other than travel time and cost, which is why most forecasting models under-perform on it, and the recommended treatment is market segmentation with stated-preference models that separate reaction to time savings by segment - including segments sensitive to travel stress and to environmental preference. Ferry uptake is concentrated among middle-to-high-income workers with a pre-existing preference for ferry-served routes.
factors.magnitude: literature: ferry choice is dominated by attitudinal and segment effects rather than time and cost; uptake concentrated in middle-to-high income
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Ferry is normally a hand-segmented mode in four-step practice; no agent-based platform in the survey attempts a behavioural ferry model.
factors.query: E Ferry: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Truck / freight: commodity, time windows, vehicle class
factors.what_research_says: Agent-based freight practice models the chain from shipment to tour: SimMobility Freight simulates commodity contracts, logistics and vehicle operation planning and parking decisions fully disaggregately, with a pre-day logistics module covering shipment requirement definition, time-window selection, carrier selection and vehicle operation planning, and ten time-window categories by time of day and duration. Calibration is screenline-based and two-step.
factors.magnitude: literature: full chain is shipment -> time window -> carrier -> vehicle operation plan -> tour; ~10 time-window categories in practice; screenline-based two-step calibration
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: SimMobility Freight is the reference implementation; MATSim's freight contrib (Schroeder and Liedtke) adds carrier agents to the same mobsim as passengers.
factors.query: E Truck / freight: commodity, time windows, vehicle class: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The road-side effect of a freight train is the level-crossing closure, and its length is set by warning-time design as much as by the train: at investigated Australian crossings warning times could be cut by 10-40 s per activation, freight trains run below line speed and so hold the boom longer than passenger trains, and closures at peak produce queue spillback into adjacent signalised intersections; a Brisbane simulation study of seven problem crossings tested treatments on exactly these delays.
factors.magnitude: literature: closure per activation is warning time plus train passage; 10-40 s of the warning time is removable; freight closures are longer than passenger closures
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: No agent-based city model simulates freight trains as vehicles; Aimsun/Vissim represent crossings as timed signal closures, which is what this model does with change events.
factors.query: ARTC Hunter Valley coal train frequency and average crossing occupation time per train at St James Road / Clyde Street

factors.what_research_says: Route choice is estimated on GPS-observed routes with path-size logit corrections for overlapping paths; length coefficients turn negative only once infrastructure attributes enter the model, and the adaptive path-size logit resolves the inconsistency of earlier forms. In iterative agent simulation the route set is co-evolved, not enumerated. No transferable share-choosing-shortest-path magnitude was recovered.
factors.magnitude: unknown (mechanism established; no central tendency for the shortest-path share)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: SUMO/Aimsun iterate dynamic user equilibrium; MATSim ReRoute co-evolves the plan set; ActivitySim delegates to assignment.
factors.query: Share of GPS-observed car routes equal to the shortest-time path in an urban network (a benchmark for ReRoute fidelity)

factors.what_research_says: Cruising for parking is a measured, large phenomenon: 3.5-14 minutes to find a curb space in congested downtowns, 8-74% of the traffic stream cruising (over 70% in recent work), and search time up to 40% of total travel time. A price that holds roughly one vacancy in eight removes the incentive to cruise and drives search time to zero.
factors.magnitude: literature: 3.5-14 min search; 8-74% of central traffic cruising; 12.5% vacancy threshold removes search entirely
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim's parking contribs simulate occupancy and search per facility; Aimsun and Vissim model parking search as a route behaviour; ActivitySim uses a terminal-time skim.
factors.query: F Parking search and occupancy: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Denied boarding and in-vehicle crowding are the same evidence base: Wardman and Whelan's 208 valuations give a seated multiplier of 1.19 and a standing multiplier of 2.32, i.e. a minute standing in a crowded vehicle costs more than twice a minute seated in an empty one, and the standing multiplier is of the same order as walk and wait multipliers.
factors.magnitude: literature: standing crowding multiplier ~2.32, seated ~1.19
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Visum and Emme price crowding inside the transit assignment and can deny boarding at capacity; MATSim denies boarding physically when a vehicle is full but does not price the crowding that precedes it.
factors.query: F Boarding, denied boarding and crowding: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Pooled matching is measured on platforms, not households: New York taxi pooling reached a 13% match rate on an ordinary day with passengers accepting up to 400 s of delay for up to 49% cost saving, a Chengdu ride-pooling dataset reached an 86.6% match with a 0.12 detour ratio, and driver detours of ~9.2 min are reported when matching riders to drivers with nearby destinations; longer response windows produce better groups and smaller detours. None of this is a household-lift tolerance.
factors.magnitude: literature (platform pooling only): match rates 13-87% by service design; accepted delay ~400 s; detour ratio ~0.12
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim DRT and BEAM implement insertion-heuristic pooling; no comparable project matches a household lift physically.
factors.query: Acceptable detour and wait for an intra-household lift (chauffeur time budget) - a household, not a platform, study

factors.factor: Network detail: lanes, capacity, speed zones, gradient
factors.what_research_says: The capacity defaults have a benchmark: the Highway Capacity Manual base saturation flow is 1,900 passenger cars per hour per lane, with practice reporting 1,800-2,000 pcu/h/lane for a single lane and arterial capacity estimated from 1,900 per lane; Austroads capacity guidance carries the same base. Downscaled agent simulations then scale flow capacity with the sample and storage a little higher at small samples.
factors.magnitude: literature: base saturation flow 1,900 pc/h/lane (HCM), 1,800-2,000 in practice; flow capacity scaled by sample share
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: SUMO and Aimsun take lanes and capacity from the network build; MATSim takes them from the OSM conversion with per-class defaults and scales by sample.
factors.query: Measured saturation flows at Newcastle SCATS sites (TfNSW) to replace the A.road.capacity_default convention

factors.factor: Signals: adaptive control and transit priority
factors.what_research_says: Adaptive control and transit signal priority are separately measured and both are material: SCATS evaluations report PM weekday travel-time reductions averaging 3.9% and weekend 1.9%, with adaptive strategies up to 29% in the widest reported range and 6-11% in Toronto; TSP reduces transit delay 30-40% and transit travel time 2-6%, with a measured 53% and 43% cut in average bus delay at two studied intersections against 14-16% increases in major-phase delay.
factors.magnitude: literature: SCATS travel-time savings ~2-11% typical; TSP transit delay -30 to -53%, transit travel time -2 to -6%
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Vissim, Aimsun and SUMO implement adaptive control and TSP as controller logic; MATSim requires the signals contrib, which few published scenarios run.
factors.query: G Signals: adaptive control and transit priority: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Dwell is a linear function of passenger flow, not a constant: TCQSM estimates it from alighting and boarding counts, a per-passenger service time and a door-opening constant, with service times of 4.5 s (exact change into the farebox), 2 s (visual inspection) and 1.75 s (no fare payment); a calibrated model gives a 5.14 s base plus 3.48 s per boarding and 1.70 s per alighting, with small diminishing marginal effects.
factors.magnitude: literature: dwell approximately 5.1 s base + 3.5 s per boarding + 1.7 s per alighting; fare-payment method moves per-passenger service time from 1.75 s to 4.5 s
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Visum and Emme use load-dependent dwell in transit assignment; MATSim's transit engine applies a fixed or schedule-derived dwell unless a contrib replaces it.
factors.query: G Transit operations: dwell, headway, capacity: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: MATSim's default link is a spatial FIFO queue with two parameters, flow capacity and storage capacity, and no intra-link interaction; the passing-queue extension lets faster vehicles overtake slower ones within a link so that, when walking and cycling are simulated on the road, pedestrians and cyclists do not block cars in the queue - the AToM Melbourne model documents this as the required setting for a multimodal network.
factors.magnitude: literature: no coefficient - a discipline choice; FIFO blocks a queue behind the slowest agent, PassingQ does not
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim (FIFO by default, PassingQ or holes optionally); SUMO and Aimsun use car-following models where passing is physical.
factors.query: Parametric calibration of the MATSim queue model (flow/storage) against observed link flows - transferable factors

factors.what_research_says: External and through trips are surveyed at the cordon: the object of an external cordon survey is the trips that originate outside the region and end inside it or pass through, and regional practice forecasts them with Fratar or gravity models calibrated on cordon counts and updated from census journey-to-work flows; Australian guidance (ATAP) treats the external zone system as part of model design. No transferable through-share magnitude was found - it is a property of the cordon geometry.
factors.magnitude: unknown (no transferable through-traffic share; cordon-specific by construction)
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every regional model carries external stations with cordon-count-calibrated I-E, E-I and E-E trips; MATSim scenarios add boundary agents in the demand builder.
factors.query: Through-traffic share at Hunter cordon stations from TfNSW classified counts or a cordon origin-destination survey

factors.what_research_says: Weather is a measured share of non-recurring delay and a measured speed effect: snow, ice and fog alone cause 15% of non-recurring delay (FHWA), a light rain raises travel-time delay 12-20%, wet pavement cuts arterial speeds 10-25% and light rain cuts freeway speed 2-13%, heavy rain reduces capacity through visibility; incidents and work zones together are about 35% of non-recurring congestion, and rain compounds an incident's speed effect. The weather effect on cycling volume (4.0-4.4 K per 10%) is on the mode-choice row.
factors.magnitude: literature: light rain +12-20% delay, arterial speed -10 to -25% on wet pavement; weather ~15% and incidents ~35% of non-recurring delay
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: No mainstream city model represents incidents or weather in a base case; SUMO and Aimsun carry them as scenario overlays (capacity and speed factors).
factors.query: BoM Newcastle rain-day frequency and the measured cycling-volume response on Hunter counters

factors.what_research_says: MATSim's scoring is the Charypar-Nagel form: plan utility is the sum of activity utilities plus travel disutilities, with activity utility beta_dur * t_typ * ln(t_dur / t_0) - marginal utility of duration against a typical duration and a minimal duration below which utility is negative - and leg score built from a mode constant, a marginal disutility of travel duration, and a marginal disutility of distance. Under iteration the population's average plan score stabilises at a point where individuals cannot unilaterally improve.
factors.magnitude: literature: activity utility is logarithmic in duration against a typical duration; leg score is linear in time and distance plus a mode constant
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim and its derivatives (eqasim, BEAM) score Charypar-Nagel; ActivitySim/CT-RAMP use nested-logit utilities instead, which is a different object - a nest coefficient has no MATSim equivalent.
factors.query: H Utility form (Charypar-Nagel scoring): literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Heterogeneity in the value of time is real and income-driven, with an income elasticity of VTTS of about 0.67-0.80 - below the unity convention. MATSim's own agent-heterogeneity work treats per-agent parameter variation as a first-class scenario feature rather than an extension.
factors.magnitude: literature: income elasticity of VTTS ~0.7-0.8; heterogeneity is income-led rather than idiosyncratic
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP segment VOT into income bands inside the utility; MATSim varies marginalUtilityOfMoney per person or defines subpopulation-specific scoring parameters.
factors.query: H Heterogeneity / value-of-time segments: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The choice set in an agent-based model is generated, not enumerated: MATSim's SubtourModeChoice changes the mode of all legs of one randomly chosen subtour to a randomly chosen alternative, and offers a mode only where the choice would not require a resource to appear out of thin air - chain-based modes assume one resource per mode, initially at home. The discrete-mode-choice contrib exists for scenarios needing an explicit, estimable choice model instead.
factors.magnitude: literature: subtour-level mode changes with chain-based resource constraints; explicit choice-set generation available only through the discrete-mode-choice contrib
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP enumerate the alternatives and evaluate a nested logit; MATSim searches co-evolutionarily; eqasim bridges the two by putting a discrete choice model inside MATSim.
factors.query: H Choice-set generation and mode availability: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.factor: Learning, replanning, plan memory, innovation switch-off
factors.what_research_says: The distinction that governs convergence: while innovation is switched on - new routes, new times - the result is NOT truly stationary; if innovation is switched off the process is stationary but limited to the plans each agent holds at that moment. The plan set is the agent's choice set, and MATSim's recommended control is fractionOfIterationsToDisableInnovation rather than a per-strategy disable iteration.
factors.magnitude: literature: no stationarity while innovation runs; stationarity after switch-off but restricted to the existing plan set
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim, eqasim and BEAM all use an innovation-off tail; ActivitySim has no equivalent because it does not iterate agents against each other in the same way.
factors.query: H Learning, replanning, plan memory, innovation switch-off: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The 2025 evidence is that LLM agents can reproduce realistic travel behaviour and system-level dynamics in morning-commute settings and can serve as the agent model inside a multi-agent simulation such as MATSim; alignment techniques - few-shot learning and travel-behaviour persona loading - materially improve mode-choice accuracy and can surpass traditional discrete choice models where domain knowledge is supplied. LLM agents partially replicate human route-switching behaviour against laboratory data. The stated blocker is computational: scaling to population level.
factors.magnitude: literature: persona-aligned LLM agents match or exceed discrete choice models on mode-choice prediction in reported studies; population-scale deployment remains computationally infeasible
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: No production city twin runs LLM agents; the work is research-stage, mostly as an agent model plugged into MATSim or as a standalone route-choice study.
factors.query: H LLM-driven agents: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Practice has explicit numeric acceptance criteria: transit validation standards of about +/-9% for regional estimated-over-observed boardings and +/-20% for transit screenlines, and MDOT screenline/cutline targets of 5% and 10% for percent difference between observed and estimated volumes. The manual also warns that counts themselves vary by 10% or more from daily and seasonal variation, and recommends at least one midweek 24-hour count every two years.
factors.magnitude: literature: +/-9% regional transit boardings, +/-20% transit screenlines, 5%/10% screenline/cutline volume targets; count data itself carries >=10% variability
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every MPO model in the US validates against this manual; MATSim scenarios in the literature typically report link-count fits and rarely per-mode ridership for every mode.
factors.query: I Targets and the validation ladder: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Validation compares the model against information other than that used to estimate it; the common practice is a random split into estimation and holdout samples at 80/20 or 75/25, with out-of-sample performance indices computed on the withheld part, and MPO guidance asks for calibration and validation at every model step. What the guidance does not describe is enforcement - no surveyed practice makes the holdout unreadable by construction.
factors.magnitude: literature: 80/20 or 75/25 estimation/holdout splits; validation on data not used in estimation
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Standard in estimation of choice models; conventional rather than enforced in MPO validation; not a feature of MATSim or ActivitySim tooling.
factors.query: A travel model that pre-registers its holdout and enforces it structurally (raise-on-read) - comparator for this project's claim

factors.what_research_says: Convergence in an iterative agent model has a precise meaning and a precise trap: the process is not stationary while innovation runs, and is stationary after switch-off only within the plans agents already hold. Empirically, between-seed variation in link loads dominates the variation between the last two iterations within one seed, so a within-run stability test alone is not evidence of convergence.
factors.magnitude: literature: between-seed variation of link loads exceeds last-two-iteration within-seed variation
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim practice reads score and mode-share stability after the innovation cutoff; ActivitySim has no iterative convergence criterion of this kind.
factors.query: I Convergence criterion: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Random seeds move agent-based results materially: across 100 seeds of one MATSim scenario, relative errors of up to 10% occur even on links with large volumes, and the variation between seeds largely dominates the variation between the two last iterations within a seed. Aggregate travel times are robust after one iteration, but disaggregate results needed about 31 simulations on average to reach a robust mean.
factors.magnitude: literature: up to 10% relative link-volume error across seeds; ~31 replications for a robust disaggregate mean; between-seed >> within-seed variation
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Aimsun and Vissim require multiple seeded replications as standard practice; most published MATSim scenarios report a single seed, which is the field's most common methodological weakness.
factors.query: I Replication across seeds / run-to-run noise: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: The recommended method for agent-based models is variance-based global sensitivity analysis: because ABMs are non-linear, Sobol' indices decompose the output variance into first-order and total contributions of each parameter and its interactions, sampled with Sobol' sequences over the input space; one-at-a-time sweeps are the local, linear special case and miss interactions.
factors.magnitude: literature: no coefficient - a method; Sobol' total-order indices over a Sobol'-sequence sample, typically hundreds to thousands of runs
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Published MATSim and SUMO studies mostly do one-at-a-time sweeps of a few parameters; the ABM literature recommends Sobol' indices as routine practice.
factors.query: A published Sobol' sensitivity analysis of a MATSim scenario (which parameters dominated mode share)

factors.what_research_says: An alternative-specific constant is the net average effect of the variables the utility omits, and calibration adjusts it iteratively - run, compare modelled to observed mode shares, move the constants, repeat until the fit is acceptable. UK TAG supplementary guidance on bespoke mode choice models is the formal statement; the risk it names is that constants absorb specification error and any new alternative has no constant to inherit.
factors.magnitude: literature: no coefficient - an iterative adjustment to observed shares; the constant is the mean of the omitted variables
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim/CT-RAMP calibrate ASCs to survey shares as a routine final step; MATSim scenarios adjust mode constants by hand or, as here, declare them fixed so misfit stays visible.
factors.query: Reported ASC magnitudes (utils) for an Australian MATSim/ActivitySim city model, to bound C.asc.*

factors.what_research_says: Population synthesis is the required input to any agent model because individual-level attributes for the whole population do not exist; the established techniques are iterative proportional fitting, iterative proportional updating, combinatorial optimisation, and Markov- and fitness-based synthesis. There is no clear guideline on choosing among them, and integer conversion and the zero-cell problem are the outstanding issues.
factors.magnitude: literature: IPF/IPU/combinatorial optimisation/Markov the established families; no consensus on choice; integer conversion and zero cells the open problems
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: ActivitySim ships PopulationSim; MATSim scenarios use eqasim's synthesiser or a bespoke one; every platform in the survey treats the synthetic population as an input rather than a modelled object.
factors.query: J Population synthesis: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Household travel survey estimates are produced on a rolling basis from multiple pooled years and weighted to the ABS Estimated Resident Population for the collection year - so an HTS figure is a multi-year average, not a single-year observation. The survey's known systematic weakness is the undercount of short walk trips: every national survey from 1977 to 2022 has undercounted total walk trips by omitting short walks to stops and car parks.
factors.magnitude: literature: HTS estimates are rolling multi-year pooled and ERP-weighted; walk trips systematically undercounted in every survey series examined
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every activity-based model in the field calibrates against an HTS of this kind; the vintage-versus-base-year mismatch is universal and rarely stated.
factors.query: J Travel survey (HTS) weighting and vintage: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Smartcard data is the standard calibration source for transit and it supports high-quality validation - agent-based models calibrated on it reach R-squared around 0.85 on on-board bus volumes - but it is structurally incomplete: most datasets capture only entry and egress points with no routing information, so trip-chaining is required to infer alighting stops and identify transfers.
factors.magnitude: literature: smartcard-calibrated transit ABMs reach R^2 ~0.85 on on-board volumes; alighting and transfers must be inferred by trip-chaining
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Visum, Emme and MATSim scenarios all calibrate PT to smartcard boardings where available; per-station validation for every mode is uncommon.
factors.query: J Smartcard (Opal) and station counts: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: Traffic counts are not a fixed truth: counts alone vary by 10% or more from daily and seasonal variation, and FHWA recommends a minimum of one midweek 24-hour count at least every two years to obtain a typical ADT estimate. Validation percentages are therefore reported by functional class and against screenlines rather than link by link.
factors.magnitude: literature: >=10% intrinsic variability in count data; validation reported by functional class and screenline, not per link
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Every four-step and ABM practice validates on counts; MATSim scenarios in the literature report link-count scatter as the primary validation.
factors.query: J Road counts: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: OpenStreetMap road completeness is about 83% globally (Barrington-Leigh and Millard-Ball 2017) and highest in cities; a 41,000 km Australian road network study finds OSM navigation performance correlates strongly with data quality, which itself tracks city population and ICT infrastructure. GTFS is the interoperable timetable format because timetables change too often for OSM; the join between the two (pt2matsim here) is the recurring failure point.
factors.magnitude: literature: OSM roads ~83% complete globally, higher in cities; Australian OSM quality tracks population and ICT
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: pt2matsim, OpenTripPlanner and UrbanAccess join GTFS to OSM; validators (gtfs-validator) check feed integrity but not map completeness.
factors.query: OSM completeness for the Hunter region against the TfNSW road segment layer (km matched)

factors.what_research_says: Downscaling has measured limits: simulations at 25% or higher of the traveller population preserve all major urban traffic statistics, while below 10% even average statistics become unreliable, with scores and travel times the first to degrade. The scaling rule is that flowCapacityFactor follows the sample share and storageCapacityFactor is set a little higher at samples of 10% or below; in one published scenario a 1% population needed a 2% flow capacity factor to reproduce the observed travel-distance distribution.
factors.magnitude: literature: >=25% preserves all major traffic statistics; below 10% even averages are unreliable; storage capacity factor set above flow at small samples
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: MATSim, SUMO and BEAM all scale link capacities with the sample; the field's usual practice is 1-10%, and 25% is at the high end of published scenarios.
factors.query: K Sample fraction and scaling rules: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it

factors.what_research_says: There is no standard iteration count: the process is run until the average population score stabilises, simple car-only scenarios converge fast, complex multimodal ones sometimes do not converge by iteration 100, one published scenario converged at iteration 164 and others run 500; because the simulation is stochastic, deterministic convergence criteria do not apply.
factors.magnitude: literature: 100-500 iterations in published scenarios; one converged at 164; no multimodal twelve-mode benchmark
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Published MATSim scenarios commonly run 100-500 iterations with an innovation-off tail; eqasim and BEAM likewise.
factors.query: Iteration counts and post-cutoff windows reported by multimodal MATSim city scenarios with PT and active modes

factors.what_research_says: Run-to-run reproducibility is not achievable by fixing a seed alone in this class of model: across 100 seeds relative errors up to 10% occur on high-volume links, and between-seed variation dominates the last-two-iteration within-seed variation. Reporting a single seeded run is therefore reporting one draw from a distribution.
factors.magnitude: literature: up to 10% relative link-volume error across seeds; between-seed variation dominates within-seed
factors.how_leading_simulators_do_it: Aimsun and Vissim require multiple replications; most published MATSim scenarios report one seed and do not state the noise floor.
factors.query: K Reproducibility of a run: literature magnitude and how MATSim / ActivitySim / eqasim implement it
